paras.text: The Islamic Republic of Pakistan is a democratic and federal parliamentary country in South Asia. After gaining independence on fourteenth August 1947, three constitutions, of 1956, 1962 and 1973, played a role in the constitutional evolution of Pakistan. At present the Constitution of 1973 is in force with several amendments. The foundations of the political system of the Government of Pakistan are as follows.

Thus the system of government of Pakistan was also established on the basis of democratic ideologies. Pakistan was achieved under an ideology which is also called the Ideology of Pakistan. Before independence Pakistan was explained through the slogan: “What does Pakistan mean? There is no god but Allah.” This ideology was basically presented by Allama Muhammad Iqbal in December 1930 at Allahabad while presiding over the annual session of the All India Muslim League. Through the Lahore Resolution of 23 March 1940 this concept was made clearer. That is, the creation of Pakistan took place on the basis of an ideology, and that ideology was the establishment of a separate homeland for the Muslims of Pakistan and India; the ideology of Islam, i.e. Pakistan would be a Muslim state established in the Muslim-majority areas of Pakistan and India. The basis of the constitution and government of this country would be placed on the opinion of the Muslims living in it. Government of Pakistan

Foundations of the structure of the Government of Pakistan

The Islamic Republic of Pakistan is a democratic and federal parliamentary country in South Asia. After gaining independence on fourteenth August 1947, three constitutions, of 1956, 1962 and 1973, played a role in the constitutional evolution of Pakistan. At present the Constitution of 1973 is in force with several amendments. The foundations of the political system of the Government of Pakistan are as follows.

1. Ideology

At the time of the creation of Pakistan different forms of government were prevalent in different countries on the basis of different ideologies, such as democratic ideologies and socialist ideologies etc. Before the creation of Pakistan the system of government prevailing in the subcontinent of Pakistan and India was established on the pattern of the British government, and in Britain the system of government had been built on the basis of democratic ideologies. Thus the system of government of Pakistan was also established on the basis of democratic ideologies. Pakistan was achieved under an ideology which is also called the Ideology of Pakistan. Before independence Pakistan was explained through the slogan: “What does Pakistan mean? There is no god but Allah.” This ideology was basically presented by Allama Muhammad Iqbal in December 1930 at Allahabad while presiding over the annual session of the All India Muslim League. Through the Lahore Resolution of 23 March 1940 this concept was made clearer. That is, the creation of Pakistan took place on the basis of an ideology, and that ideology was the establishment of a separate homeland for the Muslims of Pakistan and India; the ideology of Islam, i.e. Pakistan would be a Muslim state established in the Muslim-majority areas of Pakistan and India. The basis of the constitution and government of this country would be placed on the opinion of the Muslims living in it. On 10 August 1947 the first session of the Constituent Assembly was held in Karachi, in which, speaking, the Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah said that Pakistan would be a free, sovereign Muslim state where there would be religious freedom, i.e. everyone would have complete freedom to go to their places of worship. paras.text: Pakistan has historically also been a unit. Today’s Pakistan is a step towards the ancient civilisation of South Asia, the Indus Valley civilisation (2500–1700 BC). The River Indus still holds the same position today that ancient history gave it. The River Indus is considered the bloodstream of Pakistan, and the historic civilisation of the Indus Valley is the identity of Pakistan. This region remained part of the Mughal Empire and, from about the middle of the nineteenth century, part of the British colonial system. The British government was based on parliamentary democracy; therefore governmental evolution in the subcontinent and the democratic form of government were founded on parliamentary democracy. To introduce the democratic system in the subcontinent the British government enforced various constitutional and legal reforms, for example the Government of India Acts of 1909, 1919 and 1935. Under these reforms law-making institutions were established, for whose formation an electoral system was gradually introduced and Indians were given representation in these institutions step by step. In this way the foundation of representative democracy was laid. The subcontinent gained independence from the British in 1947. The present political system of Pakistan is the evolutionary fruit and continuation of that democratic system. In historical terms these people faced the same kind of problems for a long time. Historically these people struggled jointly for the attainment of independence and bore hardships. Of the present provinces of Pakistan, Sindh, Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Sarhad) already existed, whereas Balochistan was given the status of a province after independence. … the Objectives Resolution was passed, in which the sovereignty of Allah Almighty was acknowledged. In this way Islam was declared the official religion of the country in almost every constitution. In the Constitution of 1973 very many Islamic provisions have been included.

2. History

Pakistan has historically also been a unit. Today’s Pakistan is a step towards the ancient civilisation of South Asia, the Indus Valley civilisation (2500–1700 BC). The River Indus still holds the same position today that ancient history gave it. The River Indus is considered the bloodstream of Pakistan, and the historic civilisation of the Indus Valley is the identity of Pakistan. This region remained part of the Mughal Empire and, from about the middle of the nineteenth century, part of the British colonial system. The British government was based on parliamentary democracy; therefore governmental evolution in the subcontinent and the democratic form of government were founded on parliamentary democracy. To introduce the democratic system in the subcontinent the British government enforced various constitutional and legal reforms, for example the Government of India Acts of 1909, 1919 and 1935. Under these reforms law-making institutions were established, for whose formation an electoral system was gradually introduced and Indians were given representation in these institutions step by step. In this way the foundation of representative democracy was laid. The subcontinent gained independence from the British in 1947. The present political system of Pakistan is the evolutionary fruit and continuation of that democratic system. In historical terms these people faced the same kind of problems for a long time. Historically these people struggled jointly for the attainment of independence and bore hardships. Of the present provinces of Pakistan, Sindh, Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Sarhad) already existed, whereas Balochistan was given the status of a province after independence. The tribal identity still exists separately as before. This historical uniformity is reflected in today’s constitution and the structure of government.

… the Objectives Resolution was passed, in which the sovereignty of Allah Almighty was acknowledged. In this way Islam was declared the official religion of the country in almost every constitution. In the Constitution of 1973 very many Islamic provisions have been included.

2. History

Pakistan has historically also been a unit. Today’s Pakistan is a step towards the ancient civilisation of South Asia, the Indus Valley civilisation (2500–1700 BC). The River Indus still holds the same position today that ancient history gave it. The River Indus is considered the bloodstream of Pakistan, and the historic civilisation of the Indus Valley is the identity of Pakistan. This region remained part of the Mughal Empire and, from about the middle of the nineteenth century, part of the British colonial system. The British government was based on parliamentary democracy; therefore governmental evolution in the subcontinent and the democratic form of government were founded on parliamentary democracy. To introduce the democratic system in the subcontinent the British government enforced various constitutional and legal reforms, for example the Government of India Acts of 1909, 1919 and 1935. Under these reforms law-making institutions were established, for whose formation an electoral system was gradually introduced and Indians were given representation in these institutions step by step. In this way the foundation of representative democracy was laid. The subcontinent gained independence from the British in 1947. The present political system of Pakistan is the evolutionary fruit and continuation of that democratic system. In historical terms these people faced the same kind of problems for a long time. Historically these people struggled jointly for the attainment of independence and bore hardships. Of the present provinces of Pakistan, Sindh, Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Sarhad) already existed, whereas Balochistan was given the status of a province after independence. The tribal identity still exists separately as before. This historical uniformity is reflected in today’s constitution and the structure of government.

3. Culture

Pakistan is a multi-ethnic country. There are four basic linguistic and ethnic groups, i.e. Punjabi, Sindhi, Pakhtun and Baloch. Sub-groups of these groups also exist. In Pakistan the constitution and the structure of government bear a deep influence of these linguistic and ethnic groups …
